title: Embedding Prediction Helps Image Generation

paper.title: Embedding Prediction Helps Image Generation
paper.abstract: Abstract In diffusion transformers, a class label or a text prompt is embedded once, and the same condition is reused at every denoising step. We ask whether predicted embeddings can serve as this condition instead. Next-Embedding Predictive Autoregression (NEPA) trains a Transformer to predict the next continuous embedding in a sequence. In generation, the clean image follows the noisy image, so its embeddings are the next embeddings after the condition and the noisy image. We train a NEPA model to predict them all at once with Multi-Embedding Prediction , and in Embedding Conditioned Generation , a DiT generator is conditioned on these predictions, recomputed at every denoising step, so the conditioning signal adapts to the current noisy state. Experiments on class-conditional ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 study the condition of the generator, the design of Multi-Embedding Prediction, and the scaling of both models. The NEPA model adds a second network to every sampling step; with it, and combined with REPA, our final model, NEPA-DiT-XL , reaches an FID of 1.32 using about a third of the training compute of REPA.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Multi-embedding prediction. From the condition and the noisy image, the model predicts the next embeddings in the sequence, those of the clean image. Supervision is applied in embedding space; the predicted embeddings then condition a diffusion generator. Diffusion transformers have become the standard backbone for image generation ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ; Ma et al., 2024 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . Across these models, the condition enters through a fixed interface: a class label or a text prompt is embedded once, and the same condition is reused at every denoising step. It is left to the generator to work out what the condition implies for the image at hand as its state moves from noise to a clean sample. Recent work brings pretrained visual representations into this pipeline, as alignment targets for the generator’s features ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , as the latent space in which diffusion operates ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , or as intermediate generation targets ( Li et al., 2024a ) . In all of these, the condition itself stays fixed while the image evolves. We ask: can the condition itself be predicted from the current noisy image, at every denoising step? NEPA trains a Transformer to predict the next embedding in a sequence, rather than to reconstruct pixels or discrete tokens ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . Unlike a feature extractor, such a model is predictive by construction: its outputs are estimates of embeddings it has not yet seen. In generation, the sequence runs from the condition through the noisy image to the clean image, so the clean image is what comes next, and its predicted embeddings are a natural candidate for what a generator should condition on. We answer this question with Embedding Conditioned Generation (ECG): a DiT generator is conditioned on the embeddings predicted by a frozen NEPA model instead of on the raw condition, and the NEPA model is queried at every denoising step, so the conditioning signal adapts to the current noisy state. The NEPA model is trained with Multi-Embedding Prediction (MEP), which extends NEPA to predict the next several embeddings at once, as multi-token prediction does for tokens in language modeling ( Gloeckle et al., 2024 ) ; it reads the condition and the noisy image and predicts the embeddings of the clean image (Figure 1 ). On class-conditional ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , we compare NEPA predictions with networks of the same size trained in other ways, and study the design of Multi-Embedding Prediction and the scaling of both models. Combined with REPA, our final model, NEPA-DiT-XL, reaches an FID of 1.32 . We highlight the main contributions of this paper below: • We propose Embedding Conditioned Generation, which conditions a DiT generator on the clean embeddings predicted by a NEPA model from the condition and the noisy image, recomputed at every denoising step. • We train the NEPA model with Multi-Embedding Prediction, which extends NEPA to predict the embeddings of the whole clean image at once. • On class-conditional ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , we study the condition of the generator, the design of Multi-Embedding Prediction, and the scaling of both models; combined with REPA, NEPA-DiT-XL reaches an FID of 1.32.

sections.heading: 2.1 Diffusion Models and Representations for Generation
sections.text: Denoising diffusion models have become a dominant framework for image generation ( Song & Ermon, 2019 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ; Nichol & Dhariwal, 2021 ; Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ) , supported by faster samplers ( Song et al., 2021a ; Lu et al., 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ) and by flow-based formulations ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . Latent diffusion models operate in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder to reduce the computational cost ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Esser et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., 2025b ; Yao et al., 2025 ) , while diffusion transformers replace U-Net denoisers with more scalable architectures ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ; Bao et al., 2023 ) . Text-to-image models further improve these systems through stronger architectures, flow-based objectives, and text conditioning ( Nichol et al., 2022 ; Ramesh et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ; Balaji et al., 2023 ; Podell et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024b ; Chen et al., 2024a ; Esser et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024c ; Peng et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) . Beyond synthesis, diffusion models have been adapted to text-guided image manipulation and editing ( Meng et al., 2022 ; Hertz et al., 2023 ; Mokady et al., 2023 ; Brooks et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2024 ) , to spatially controlled generation ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , and to temporally consistent video generation ( Ho et al., 2022 ; Guo et al., 2024 ; Xia et al., 2024 ) . Pretrained visual representations have been brought into this pipeline as generation targets ( Li et al., 2024a ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Kouzelis et al., 2025b ) , alignment signals for diffusion features ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Tian et al., 2026 ; Leng et al., 2025 ) , and the generative latent space ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Tong et al., 2026 ; Singh et al., 2026 ) . In these models, the class or text condition is injected by adaLN ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) or joint attention ( Esser et al., 2024 ) and stays fixed across denoising steps. Unified multimodal models condition a diffusion decoder on embeddings produced by a language model ( Sun et al., 2024b ; Ge et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025a ) , but these embeddings are likewise computed once before sampling. Self-conditioning ( Chen et al., 2023 ) feeds the estimate of the clean sample from the previous sampling step back into the denoiser, and RIN ( Jabri et al., 2023 ) carries latent states across steps; both reuse the estimates of the denoiser itself. We condition the generator on the predictions of a separate NEPA model, trained with its own embedding prediction objective and recomputed from the current noisy input at every step.

sections.heading: 2.2 Predictive Representation Learning
sections.text: Self-supervised visual learning has progressed from handcrafted pretext tasks ( Doersch et al., 2015 ; Noroozi & Favaro, 2016 ; Zhang et al., 2016 ; Gidaris et al., 2018 ) to contrastive and self-distillation methods ( van den Oord et al., 2019 ; He et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2020 ; Grill et al., 2020 ; Caron et al., 2020 ; Caron et al., 2021 ; Zhou et al., 2022 ) and to masked reconstruction approaches that predict pixels, tokens, or visual features ( Bao et al., 2022 ; He et al., 2022 ; Xie et al., 2022 ; Wei et al., 2022 ; Baevski et al., 2022 ) . Generative image models instead learn by predicting discrete or continuous visual tokens, either autoregressively or through masked and progressively refined prediction ( van den Oord et al., 2017 ; Esser et al., 2021 ; Yu et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2022 ; Chang et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2024a ; Li et al., 2024b ) . However, pixel and discrete-token prediction can emphasize low-level details or tokenizer-specific structure. Predictive representation learning avoids direct reconstruction by predicting targets in a learned embedding space: JEPA and I-JEPA predict masked target representations from visible context, and V-JEPA extends this principle to spatiotemporal prediction ( LeCun, 2022 ; Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ; Assran et al., 2025 ) . NEPA further combines representation prediction with causal modeling by replacing the next-token prediction of language models ( Radford et al., 2019 ; Brown et al., 2020 ) with next-embedding prediction ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . Our Multi-Embedding Prediction extends NEPA to predict several embeddings at once, analogous to multi-token prediction in language modeling ( Gloeckle et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Our method has two stages. First, we train a NEPA model with Multi-Embedding Prediction to predict clean image embeddings from condition tokens and noisy image embeddings. Second, we train a DiT generator with Embedding Conditioned Generation , where the frozen NEPA model produces predictive embeddings at each denoising step and the DiT uses them as its condition.

sections.heading: 3.1 Preliminaries
sections.text: Next-embedding predictive autoregression. NEPA replaces next-token prediction with next-embedding prediction ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . An input 𝐱 \mathbf{x} is split into N N non-overlapping patches by a convolutional patch embedding layer f f , giving a sequence of continuous embeddings 𝐳 = f ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) \mathbf{z}=f(\mathbf{x}) . sections.heading: 3.2 Multi-Embedding Prediction
sections.text: Figure 2: Multi-token vs. multi-embedding prediction. Both predict several items at once. (a) Tokens are discrete, so hidden states are decoded into tokens by output heads. (b) Embeddings are continuous, so the outputs of the model are the predictions themselves. In both, the same context predicts all targets in one forward pass. NEPA predicts one next embedding at a time. In language modeling, predicting several future tokens at once improves over next-token prediction ( Gloeckle et al., 2024 ) . Predicting one embedding at a time is similarly limiting when the next embeddings form a group that is needed together, such as the patch embeddings of an image. Multi-Embedding Prediction (MEP) extends NEPA to predict the next K K embeddings simultaneously from the same context. Given the context embeddings 𝐳 ≤ n \mathbf{z}_{\leq n} , the model predicts the next K K embeddings in a single forward pass: 𝐩 n + 1 : n + K = h θ ( 𝐳 ≤ n ) , ℒ MEP = 1 K ∑ k = 1 K 𝒟 ( 𝐳 n + k , 𝐩 n + k ) . \mathbf{p}_{n+1:n+K}=h_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{\leq n}),\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MEP}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{z}_{n+k},\mathbf{p}_{n+k}). (3) NEPA is the special case K = 1 K=1 . Like multi-token prediction, MEP predicts several items at once; it differs in predicting in embedding space rather than token space. Predicted tokens must be decoded from hidden states by output heads, whereas predicted embeddings are the outputs of the model themselves (Figure 2 ). Section 3.3 instantiates MEP for image generation.

sections.heading: 3.3 NEPA for Generation
sections.text: Figure 3: MEP for generation. The clean image embeddings are the next embeddings after the condition and the noisy image; the output at each noisy patch predicts the embedding that follows it. Generation produces an image through a sequence of states: from the condition, through a noisy image, to the clean image. We write this as a sequence of embeddings, the condition, then the N N patch embeddings of the noisy image, then the N N patch embeddings of the clean image. In this sequence, the clean embeddings are the next N N embeddings after the condition and the noisy image, and we train a NEPA model to predict them with MEP, taking K = N K=N . The sequence is ordered by generation state rather than by patch position, so the embedding that follows noisy patch i i is clean patch i i . MEP predicts all N N embeddings of the clean image in one forward pass, each from the full context of the condition and the noisy image. The model is defined by three choices: the sequence and its readout, an attention mask with the condition as a causal prefix, and an InfoNCE loss. Given a clean input 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} , we sample a noise level t t and construct the noisy input 𝐱 t = ( 1 − t ) ​ 𝐱 0 + t ​ ϵ \mathbf{x}_{t}=(1-t)\mathbf{x}_{0}+t\boldsymbol{\epsilon} . Both are patchified by the embedding layer into noisy and clean patch embeddings, 𝐳 t = f ⁡ ( 𝐱 t ) \mathbf{z}_{t}=f(\mathbf{x}_{t}) and 𝐳 0 = f ⁡ ( 𝐱 0 ) \mathbf{z}_{0}=f(\mathbf{x}_{0}) . As in NEPA, the targets come from the model’s own patch embedding layer f f , which is learned jointly with the model. The targets are compared through InfoNCE rather than regressed: the model only has to tell each patch apart from the other patches of the image, and the remaining detail is left to the generator. The noise level is sampled uniformly, t ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) , so that a single model covers every denoising step at inference, and the condition is replaced by a null token with probability 0.1, so that the same model also provides the unconditional predictions used for classifier-free guidance (Section 3.4 ). As shown in Figure 3 , the NEPA model h θ h_{\theta} reads the condition c c , a begin-of-image token ⟨ boi ⟩ \langle\mathrm{boi}\rangle , and the noisy embeddings, and predicts the next N N embeddings, the clean image: 𝐩 = h θ ​ ( [ c , ⟨ boi ⟩ ] , 𝐳 t ) , ℒ MEP = 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝐳 0 , 𝐩 ) . \mathbf{p}=h_{\theta}([c,\langle\mathrm{boi}\rangle],\mathbf{z}_{t}),\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MEP}}=\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{z}_{0},\mathbf{p}). (4) This is Equation 3 with the context [ c , ⟨ boi ⟩ , 𝐳 t ] [c,\langle\mathrm{boi}\rangle,\mathbf{z}_{t}] and the next K = N K=N embeddings 𝐳 0 \mathbf{z}_{0} . As in NEPA, where the output at each position predicts the embedding that follows it, the output at noisy patch i i predicts its next embedding 𝐳 0 , i \mathbf{z}_{0,i} . The noise level sets the difficulty: at t = 1 t=1 the noisy image carries no information and the clean image must be predicted from the condition alone, whereas as t → 0 t\to 0 the noisy image approaches the clean one. Attention mask. The condition tokens and ⟨ boi ⟩ \langle\mathrm{boi}\rangle form a causal prefix that never attends to image tokens. The image tokens of the noisy image attend to the whole prefix and to each other, and every prediction uses the full spatial context of the noisy image (Figure 4 ). Since the prefix does not depend on the image, it is encoded once and cached during sampling (Section 3.4 ). Embedding prediction loss. Each prediction 𝐩 i \mathbf{p}_{i} is trained to match its next embedding 𝐳 0 , i \mathbf{z}_{0,i} . The distance 𝒟 \mathcal{D} in Equation 4 can take many forms (Section 4.1 ); we use the InfoNCE loss ( van den Oord et al., 2019 ) , with predicted embeddings as queries and clean embeddings as keys. Figure 4: Attention mask. Rows are queries and columns are keys; dark cells are masked. Figure 5: Embedding prediction loss. As illustrated in Figure 5 , the positives lie on the diagonal, pairing each 𝐩 i \mathbf{p}_{i} with 𝐳 0 , i \mathbf{z}_{0,i} , while the other patches of the same image serve as negatives: 𝒟 ( 𝐳 0 , 𝐩 ) = − 1 N ∑ i = 1 N log exp ⁡ ( 𝐩 i ⊤ ​ 𝐳 0 , i ) ∑ j = 1 N exp ⁡ ( 𝐩 i ⊤ ​ 𝐳 0 , j ) . \mathcal{D}(\mathbf{z}_{0},\mathbf{p})=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log\frac{\exp(\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{z}_{0,i})}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{z}_{0,j})}. (5) After this stage, the NEPA model maps the condition and the noisy image to predicted clean image embeddings.

sections.heading: 3.4 Embedding Conditioned Generation
sections.text: The second stage trains the generator G ϕ G_{\phi} with the NEPA model h θ h_{\theta} frozen as its conditioning module. The NEPA model predicts the clean embeddings, while the generator learns the denoising vector field. At each denoising step, the current noisy input 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} is first fed into the NEPA model, which outputs predictive embeddings 𝐩 t = h θ ​ ( [ c , ⟨ boi ⟩ ] , f ⁡ ( 𝐱 t ) ) \mathbf{p}_{t}=h_{\theta}([c,\langle\mathrm{boi}\rangle],f(\mathbf{x}_{t})) . The generator follows DiT ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) (details in Appendix C ), except that it is conditioned on 𝐩 t \mathbf{p}_{t} through the MM-DiT blocks of SD3 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) : the predicted embeddings and the noisy latent tokens are processed with separate weights and exchange information through joint attention, followed by single-stream blocks on the concatenated sequence. The generator receives the condition only through 𝐩 t \mathbf{p}_{t} and has no separate class embedding; the timestep enters through adaLN modulation, as in DiT. The training loss is the weighted flow-matching loss ℒ ECG = 𝔼 𝐱 0 , ϵ , t , c ​ [ w ⁡ ( t ) ​ ‖ 𝐯 t − G ϕ ​ ( 𝐱 t , t , 𝐩 t ) ‖ 2 ] . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ECG}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{\epsilon},t,c}\Big[\,w(t)\,\big\|\,\mathbf{v}_{t}-G_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\mathbf{p}_{t})\,\big\|^{2}\Big]. (6) During this stage, gradients update only the generator; the VAE and the NEPA model remain frozen. Condition caching. Because the condition prefix never attends to image tokens, its key-value cache in the NEPA model is computed once before the denoising loop and reused at every step; only the image tokens are re-encoded as 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} changes. Classifier-free guidance ( Ho & Salimans, 2021 ) . During training, we randomly replace the condition c c with a learned null token. At inference, the unconditional branch feeds the null token to the NEPA model, which yields 𝐩 t ∅ \mathbf{p}_{t}^{\varnothing} , and guidance is applied to the velocities predicted by the generator: 𝐯 ^ cond = G ϕ ( 𝐱 t , t , 𝐩 t ) , 𝐯 ^ uncond = G ϕ ( 𝐱 t , t , 𝐩 t ∅ ) , 𝐯 ^ cfg = 𝐯 ^ uncond + s ⋅ ( 𝐯 ^ cond − 𝐯 ^ uncond ) , \begin{gathered}\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathrm{cond}}=G_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\mathbf{p}_{t}),\qquad\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathrm{uncond}}=G_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\mathbf{p}_{t}^{\varnothing}),\\ \hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathrm{cfg}}=\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathrm{uncond}}+s\cdot(\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathrm{cond}}-\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathrm{uncond}}),\end{gathered} (7) where s s is the guidance scale.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate our framework on class-conditional ImageNet-1K generation at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution. At small scale, Section 4.1 ablates the design of Multi-Embedding Prediction and Section 4.2 compares conditions of the generator; Section 4.3 then scales up the NEPA model and the generator, and Section 4.4 compares our final model with prior work. Setup. Following ADM ( Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ) , images are center-cropped to 256 × 256 256\times 256 and encoded by the frozen SD-VAE ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) into 32 × 32 × 4 32\times 32\times 4 latents. The NEPA model follows Xu et al. (2025) and the generator follows DiT ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) , each at B, L, and XL scale; NEPA-DiT-B/L/XL denotes a NEPA model paired with a DiT-B/L/XL generator. Unless stated otherwise, the NEPA model is NEPA-XL with patch size 4, and the generator uses patch size 2. The NEPA model is trained with Multi-Embedding Prediction for 240 epochs, then frozen while the generator is trained with the flow-matching loss for 400K iterations (80 epochs), both at batch size 256. Appendix C gives further details. Evaluation. We report the Fréchet Inception Distance on 50K samples (FID-50K), computed with the ADM evaluation suite and its ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 reference batch ( Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ) . Unless stated otherwise, ablation and scaling experiments sample with a 64-step ODE solver and no classifier-free guidance; the sampling setup of our final model is given in Section 4.4 .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We have shown that predictive embeddings can serve as the condition of an image generator. In Embedding Conditioned Generation, a DiT generator is conditioned at every denoising step on the clean-image embeddings that a NEPA model, trained with Multi-Embedding Prediction, predicts from the condition and the current noisy image. On ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , combined with REPA, NEPA-DiT-XL reaches an FID of 1.32 with the 250-step SDE sampler and 1.57 with the 96-step ODE sampler, trained with about a third of REPA’s compute even though it trains and runs two networks. Code and model weights will be released. Future work is discussed in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Appendix A Relation to Other Methods
sections.text: Relation to RepFusion. RepFusion ( Pan et al., 2026a ) also conditions a diffusion transformer on the outputs of a model that reads the noisy input at every denoising step. It builds on two existing components: the latent space of a representation autoencoder ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , which it adopts so that noisy latents are compatible with pretrained language-model priors, and a pretrained multimodal LLM, which it repurposes as the encoder of noisy representations. Our NEPA model depends on neither. It is trained from scratch with Multi-Embedding Prediction directly on the latents of a standard VAE, so the conditioning interface is defined by a training objective rather than by an existing model. The same recipe can therefore be applied to any Transformer as the NEPA model and to any generator that accepts conditioning tokens. Relation to DDT. DDT ( Wang et al., 2026b ) also splits the generator into a condition encoder that reads the noisy latent and a velocity decoder conditioned on the encoder output. The two are trained jointly: the encoder is supervised indirectly through the velocity loss of the decoder, together with a REPA alignment to DINOv2 features. Our NEPA model is instead trained separately to predict the clean embeddings of the image and is then frozen, so the condition is a representation learned with its own objective rather than an intermediate feature of the generator. DDT also shares the encoder output between adjacent denoising steps to accelerate sampling, and Table 14 studies the corresponding choice for our NEPA model. Relation to 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} -prediction and self-conditioning. A diffusion model can be parameterized to predict the clean sample 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Karras et al., 2022 ) , and JiT ( Li & He, 2026 ) predicts it directly with a Transformer on raw pixels. Self-conditioning ( Chen et al., 2023 ) and RIN ( Jabri et al., 2023 ) feed such an estimate, or the latent state behind it, back into the same denoiser at the next step. In both cases the estimate comes from the denoiser itself and is trained by its denoising loss. Our NEPA model is a separate network, trained with its own embedding prediction objective and then frozen, and its predictions are recomputed from the current noisy input at every step. Table 7 includes, in the same setting, a network of the same architecture trained end to end with the generator by flow matching, and the same network pretrained as a flow-matching model and then frozen.

sections.heading: Appendix B Future Work
sections.text: Text conditions. Text-to-image models either encode the prompt once with a separate text encoder ( Saharia et al., 2022 ; Chen et al., 2024b ; Esser et al., 2024 ) , which cannot adapt to the evolving noisy image and often fixes the length of the condition, or process the prompt together with the image in a single unified model ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , where the condition and the image share one backbone. A NEPA model could instead read the whole prompt before the noisy image and predict the clean image embeddings from both, as it does for class labels in this paper. Unified models. Since the NEPA model is an autoregressive Transformer, a single NEPA model could in principle serve both as a language model with an output head and as the conditioning model of a DiT generator. Studying text conditions, other latent spaces, and higher resolutions are directions for future work.

Throughout the experiments, the generator matches DiT ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) in depth, width, and number of heads, but uses MM-DiT blocks ( Esser et al., 2024 ) : the first blocks are two-stream and process the predicted embeddings and the latent tokens with separate weights, and the remaining blocks are single-stream blocks on the concatenated sequence. The NEPA model is kept frozen when training the generator. We use mixed precision (bfloat16) with gradient clipping at 1.0 for both stages, and keep an EMA of the generator weights with decay 0.9999. The timestep of the generator is sampled from a logit-normal distribution with zero mean and unit variance ( Esser et al., 2024 ) . We use the stabilityai/sd-vae-ft-mse VAE ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) for encoding images during training and the stabilityai/sd-vae-ft-ema VAE for decoding samples. For the REPA projector, we use a three-layer MLP with SiLU activations and hidden dimension 2,048, following Yu et al. (2025) . We provide a detailed hyperparameter setup in Tables 11 and 12 . Pretrained encoder. For REPA, we use the official DINOv2-B checkpoint with registers. ImageNet-1K accuracy. The accuracy reported in Tables 1 and 8 is the top-1 accuracy of the NEPA model after fine-tuning it for ImageNet-1K classification with the fine-tuning recipe of NEPA ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . Sampling. For the system-level comparison, we use the SDE Euler-Maruyama sampler of SiT ( Ma et al., 2024 ) with 250 steps, or the Euler ODE sampler with 96 steps, and apply classifier-free guidance with a scale of 3.6 only for t ∈ [ 0.4 , 1 ] t\in[0.4,1] ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) . Other results use the Euler ODE sampler, and the number of steps is given with each table. DiT baseline. The DiT-B baseline uses the same generator as NEPA-DiT-B, but conditions it directly on a learned class embedding instead of the embeddings predicted by the NEPA model. The class embedding enters the text stream of the MM-DiT blocks as a single token, in place of the predicted embeddings; in both models, the timestep enters through adaLN modulation. All other settings, including the training objective, timestep distribution, and optimization, are the same (Table 12 ). Computing resources. All models are trained on NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The NEPA model is trained once for 240 epochs and is then frozen and shared by all generators; each generator is trained for 400K iterations at batch size 256 (80 epochs). Yu Affiliation: University of Michigan Abstract In diffusion transformers, a class label or a text prompt is embedded once, and the same condition is reused at every denoising step. We ask whether predicted embeddings can serve as this condition instead. Next-Embedding Predictive Autoregression (NEPA) trains a Transformer to predict the next continuous embedding in a sequence. In generation, the clean image follows the noisy image, so its embeddings are the next embeddings after the condition and the noisy image. We train a NEPA model to predict them all at once with Multi-Embedding Prediction , and in Embedding Conditioned Generation , a DiT generator is conditioned on these predictions, recomputed at every denoising step, so the conditioning signal adapts to the current noisy state. Experiments on class-conditional ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 study the condition of the generator, the design of Multi-Embedding Prediction, and the scaling of both models. The NEPA model adds a second network to every sampling step; with it, and combined with REPA, our final model, NEPA-DiT-XL , reaches an FID of 1.32 using about a third of the training compute of REPA. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Multi-embedding prediction. From the condition and the noisy image, the model predicts the next embeddings in the sequence, those of the clean image. Supervision is applied in embedding space; the predicted embeddings then condition a diffusion generator. Diffusion transformers have become the standard backbone for image generation ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ; Ma et al., 2024 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) . Across these models, the condition enters through a fixed interface: a class label or a text prompt is embedded once, and the same condition is reused at every denoising step. It is left to the generator to work out what the condition implies for the image at hand as its state moves from noise to a clean sample. Recent work brings pretrained visual representations into this pipeline, as alignment targets for the generator’s features ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , as the latent space in which diffusion operates ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , or as intermediate generation targets ( Li et al., 2024a ) . In all of these, the condition itself stays fixed while the image evolves. We ask: can the condition itself be predicted from the current noisy image, at every denoising step? NEPA trains a Transformer to predict the next embedding in a sequence, rather than to reconstruct pixels or discrete tokens ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . Unlike a feature extractor, such a model is predictive by construction: its outputs are estimates of embeddings it has not yet seen. In generation, the sequence runs from the condition through the noisy image to the clean image, so the clean image is what comes next, and its predicted embeddings are a natural candidate for what a generator should condition on. We answer this question with Embedding Conditioned Generation (ECG): a DiT generator is conditioned on the embeddings predicted by a frozen NEPA model instead of on the raw condition, and the NEPA model is queried at every denoising step, so the conditioning signal adapts to the current noisy state. The NEPA model is trained with Multi-Embedding Prediction (MEP), which extends NEPA to predict the next several embeddings at once, as multi-token prediction does for tokens in language modeling ( Gloeckle et al., 2024 ) ; it reads the condition and the noisy image and predicts the embeddings of the clean image (Figure 1 ). On class-conditional ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , we compare NEPA predictions with networks of the same size trained in other ways, and study the design of Multi-Embedding Prediction and the scaling of both models. Combined with REPA, our final model, NEPA-DiT-XL, reaches an FID of 1.32 . We highlight the main contributions of this paper below: • We propose Embedding Conditioned Generation, which conditions a DiT generator on the clean embeddings predicted by a NEPA model from the condition and the noisy image, recomputed at every denoising step. • We train the NEPA model with Multi-Embedding Prediction, which extends NEPA to predict the embeddings of the whole clean image at once. • On class-conditional ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , we study the condition of the generator, the design of Multi-Embedding Prediction, and the scaling of both models; combined with REPA, NEPA-DiT-XL reaches an FID of 1.32. 2 Related Work 2.1 Diffusion Models and Representations for Generation Denoising diffusion models have become a dominant framework for image generation ( Song & Ermon, 2019 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ; Nichol & Dhariwal, 2021 ; Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ) , supported by faster samplers ( Song et al., 2021a ; Lu et al., 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ) and by flow-based formulations ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . Latent diffusion models operate in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder to reduce the computational cost ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Esser et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., 2025b ; Yao et al., 2025 ) , while diffusion transformers replace U-Net denoisers with more scalable architectures ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ; Bao et al., 2023 ) . Text-to-image models further improve these systems through stronger architectures, flow-based objectives, and text conditioning ( Nichol et al., 2022 ; Ramesh et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ; Balaji et al., 2023 ; Podell et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024b ; Chen et al., 2024a ; Esser et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024c ; Peng et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) . Beyond synthesis, diffusion models have been adapted to text-guided image manipulation and editing ( Meng et al., 2022 ; Hertz et al., 2023 ; Mokady et al., 2023 ; Brooks et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2024 ) , to spatially controlled generation ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , and to temporally consistent video generation ( Ho et al., 2022 ; Guo et al., 2024 ; Xia et al., 2024 ) . Pretrained visual representations have been brought into this pipeline as generation targets ( Li et al., 2024a ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Kouzelis et al., 2025b ) , alignment signals for diffusion features ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Tian et al., 2026 ; Leng et al., 2025 ) , and the generative latent space ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Tong et al., 2026 ; Singh et al., 2026 ) . In these models, the class or text condition is injected by adaLN ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) or joint attention ( Esser et al., 2024 ) and stays fixed across denoising steps. Unified multimodal models condition a diffusion decoder on embeddings produced by a language model ( Sun et al., 2024b ; Ge et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025a ) , but these embeddings are likewise computed once before sampling. Self-conditioning ( Chen et al., 2023 ) feeds the estimate of the clean sample from the previous sampling step back into the denoiser, and RIN ( Jabri et al., 2023 ) carries latent states across steps; both reuse the estimates of the denoiser itself. We condition the generator on the predictions of a separate NEPA model, trained with its own embedding prediction objective and recomputed from the current noisy input at every step. 2.2 Predictive Representation Learning Self-supervised visual learning has progressed from handcrafted pretext tasks ( Doersch et al., 2015 ; Noroozi & Favaro, 2016 ; Zhang et al., 2016 ; Gidaris et al., 2018 ) to contrastive and self-distillation methods ( van den Oord et al., 2019 ; He et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2020 ; Grill et al., 2020 ; Caron et al., 2020 ; Caron et al., 2021 ; Zhou et al., 2022 ) and to masked reconstruction approaches that predict pixels, tokens, or visual features ( Bao et al., 2022 ; He et al., 2022 ; Xie et al., 2022 ; Wei et al., 2022 ; Baevski et al., 2022 ) . Generative image models instead learn by predicting discrete or continuous visual tokens, either autoregressively or through masked and progressively refined prediction ( van den Oord et al., 2017 ; Esser et al., 2021 ; Yu et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2022 ; Chang et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2024a ; Li et al., 2024b ) . However, pixel and discrete-token prediction can emphasize low-level details or tokenizer-specific structure. Predictive representation learning avoids direct reconstruction by predicting targets in a learned embedding space: JEPA and I-JEPA predict masked target representations from visible context, and V-JEPA extends this principle to spatiotemporal prediction ( LeCun, 2022 ; Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ; Assran et al., 2025 ) . NEPA further combines representation prediction with causal modeling by replacing the next-token prediction of language models ( Radford et al., 2019 ; Brown et al., 2020 ) with next-embedding prediction ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . Our Multi-Embedding Prediction extends NEPA to predict several embeddings at once, analogous to multi-token prediction in language modeling ( Gloeckle et al., 2024 ) . 3 Method Our method has two stages. First, we train a NEPA model with Multi-Embedding Prediction to predict clean image embeddings from condition tokens and noisy image embeddings. Second, we train a DiT generator with Embedding Conditioned Generation , where the frozen NEPA model produces predictive embeddings at each denoising step and the DiT uses them as its condition. 3.1 Preliminaries Next-embedding predictive autoregression. NEPA replaces next-token prediction with next-embedding prediction ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . An input 𝐱 \mathbf{x} is split into N N non-overlapping patches by a convolutional patch embedding layer f f , giving a sequence of continuous embeddings 𝐳 = f ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) \mathbf{z}=f(\mathbf{x}) . An autoregressive model h θ h_{\theta} reads the sequence and predicts, at each position, the embedding that follows it, and is trained with a distance 𝒟 \mathcal{D} in embedding space between the predictions 𝐩 \mathbf{p} and the targets 𝐳 target \mathbf{z}_{\text{target}} : 𝐩 = h θ ​ ( 𝐳 ) , ℒ NEPA = 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝐳 target , 𝐩 ) , \mathbf{p}=h_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}),\qquad\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NEPA}}=\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{z}_{\text{target}},\mathbf{p}), (1) where 𝒟 \mathcal{D} is any distance between embeddings. For images, NEPA orders the patches into a sequence under causal attention, so the target is the next patch, 𝐳 target = 𝐳 2 : N \mathbf{z}_{\text{target}}=\mathbf{z}_{2:N} . Latent diffusion and flow matching. Following latent diffusion models and DiT ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) , we perform image generation in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder: a frozen encoder ℰ \mathcal{E} maps each image to a clean latent 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} , which serves as the input to both models, and a frozen decoder maps generated latents back to images. Conventionally, c c is fixed across the sampling trajectory; we replace it with embeddings predicted by a NEPA model from both the condition c c and the current noisy image state 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} . This allows the conditioning signal to adapt throughout denoising, as described in Section 3.4 . 3.2 Multi-Embedding Prediction Figure 2: Multi-token vs. multi-embedding prediction. Both predict several items at once. (a) Tokens are discrete, so hidden states are decoded into tokens by output heads. (b) Embeddings are continuous, so the outputs of the model are the predictions themselves. In both, the same context predicts all targets in one forward pass. NEPA predicts one next embedding at a time. In language modeling, predicting several future tokens at once improves over next-token prediction ( Gloeckle et al., 2024 ) . Predicting one embedding at a time is similarly limiting when the next embeddings form a group that is needed together, such as the patch embeddings of an image. Multi-Embedding Prediction (MEP) extends NEPA to predict the next K K embeddings simultaneously from the same context. Given the context embeddings 𝐳 ≤ n \mathbf{z}_{\leq n} , the model predicts the next K K embeddings in a single forward pass: 𝐩 n + 1 : n + K = h θ ( 𝐳 ≤ n ) , ℒ MEP = 1 K ∑ k = 1 K 𝒟 ( 𝐳 n + k , 𝐩 n + k ) . \mathbf{p}_{n+1:n+K}=h_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{\leq n}),\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MEP}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{z}_{n+k},\mathbf{p}_{n+k}). (3) NEPA is the special case K = 1 K=1 . Like multi-token prediction, MEP predicts several items at once; it differs in predicting in embedding space rather than token space. Predicted tokens must be decoded from hidden states by output heads, whereas predicted embeddings are the outputs of the model themselves (Figure 2 ). Section 3.3 instantiates MEP for image generation. 3.3 NEPA for Generation Figure 3: MEP for generation. The clean image embeddings are the next embeddings after the condition and the noisy image; the output at each noisy patch predicts the embedding that follows it. Generation produces an image through a sequence of states: from the condition, through a noisy image, to the clean image. We write this as a sequence of embeddings, the condition, then the N N patch embeddings of the noisy image, then the N N patch embeddings of the clean image. In this sequence, the clean embeddings are the next N N embeddings after the condition and the noisy image, and we train a NEPA model to predict them with MEP, taking K = N K=N . The sequence is ordered by generation state rather than by patch position, so the embedding that follows noisy patch i i is clean patch i i . MEP predicts all N N embeddings of the clean image in one forward pass, each from the full context of the condition and the noisy image. The model is defined by three choices: the sequence and its readout, an attention mask with the condition as a causal prefix, and an InfoNCE loss. Given a clean input 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} , we sample a noise level t t and construct the noisy input 𝐱 t = ( 1 − t ) ​ 𝐱 0 + t ​ ϵ \mathbf{x}_{t}=(1-t)\mathbf{x}_{0}+t\boldsymbol{\epsilon} . Both are patchified by the embedding layer into noisy and clean patch embeddings, 𝐳 t = f ⁡ ( 𝐱 t ) \mathbf{z}_{t}=f(\mathbf{x}_{t}) and 𝐳 0 = f ⁡ ( 𝐱 0 ) \mathbf{z}_{0}=f(\mathbf{x}_{0}) . As in NEPA, the targets come from the model’s own patch embedding layer f f , which is learned jointly with the model. The targets are compared through InfoNCE rather than regressed: the model only has to tell each patch apart from the other patches of the image, and the remaining detail is left to the generator. The noise level is sampled uniformly, t ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) , so that a single model covers every denoising step at inference, and the condition is replaced by a null token with probability 0.1, so that the same model also provides the unconditional predictions used for classifier-free guidance (Section 3.4 ). The NEPA model predicts the clean embeddings, while the generator learns the denoising vector field. At each denoising step, the current noisy input 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} is first fed into the NEPA model, which outputs predictive embeddings 𝐩 t = h θ ​ ( [ c , ⟨ boi ⟩ ] , f ⁡ ( 𝐱 t ) ) \mathbf{p}_{t}=h_{\theta}([c,\langle\mathrm{boi}\rangle],f(\mathbf{x}_{t})) . At small scale, Section 4.1 ablates the design of Multi-Embedding Prediction and Section 4.2 compares conditions of the generator; Section 4.3 then scales up the NEPA model and the generator, and Section 4.4 compares our final model with prior work. The NEPA model follows Xu et al. (2025) and the generator follows DiT ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) , each at B, L, and XL scale; NEPA-DiT-B/L/XL denotes a NEPA model paired with a DiT-B/L/XL generator. In Embedding Conditioned Generation, a DiT generator is conditioned at every denoising step on the clean-image embeddings that a NEPA model, trained with Multi-Embedding Prediction, predicts from the condition and the current noisy image. On ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , combined with REPA, NEPA-DiT-XL reaches an FID of 1.32 with the 250-step SDE sampler and 1.57 with the 96-step ODE sampler, trained with about a third of REPA’s compute even though it trains and runs two networks.
